_comment: Every entry is one topic. `ask` lists the ways a teacher might raise it —
these are matched against, not shown — and `answer` is what comes back.
`tags` are single words that carry extra weight when scoring, which is how
'how much' finds pricing even though it shares no words with 'cost'.
{{PRICING}} and {{TRIAL_DAYS}} are filled at render time from
src/lib/plans.js, so a price can never be quoted here that the pricing
table on the page contradicts. Do not write figures into this file.
Answers use light markdown: **bold**, *italic*, and lines starting with
- for bullets. That is all the renderer understands.

topics.answer:
Murchid is an **AI lesson director** for schoolteachers, KG through Grade 12. It's built for the UAE and the Gulf, and it understands the MoE and IB curricula.

The idea in one line: *the teacher directs, Murchid drafts.*

You describe the lesson you need. Murchid writes the plan, the quiz, the homework or the slides — into your own structure, ready to edit. Nothing reaches a student until you've approved it.

Five steps, start to finish:

- **Sign in** with Google, LinkedIn, or an email and password.
- **Set up in two clicks** — upload a CV or staff card and Murchid reads your subjects, grades and school off it.
- **Describe what you need.** Attach your own material if you like: a textbook chapter, a syllabus PDF.
- **Murchid drafts it.** You edit anything, save it, and assign it to a class.
- **Marks and attendance** come back into your gradebook.

The whole loop is a school week, not a chat box.

ask: what can i make with it
topics.answer:
What you can make and manage:

- **Lesson plans** — objectives, an intro, the main activity, a conclusion, an assessment method.
- **Quizzes** — multiple choice, true/false, short answer and essay. Edit any question by hand.
- **Homework** — set it, give it to a class, see who has handed in.
- **Presentations** — slide decks built from a lesson plan.
- **Activities** — classroom activities with materials and timings.
- **My students** — a register, classes, attendance and a gradebook.
- **Planner and schedule** — a timetable you can drop a lesson plan onto.

Honestly, four things:

- **It drafts into your structure**, not a wall of text you then have to reformat.
- **It's built around a real school week** — a register, a timetable, a gradebook. Not just a box that writes.
- **It reads your own materials**, so a plan matches the book your school actually uses.
- **It's bilingual** — the whole interface works in English and Arabic, right-to-left included.

And nothing is auto-submitted. Every draft is yours to review first.

Start with a **{{TRIAL_DAYS}}-day free trial** — no card required.

After that:

{{PRICING}}

You can switch or cancel from your account at any time.

ask: do i need a credit card
topics.answer:
Yes — **{{TRIAL_DAYS}} days, free, and no card required.**

You get the full studio during the trial, not a cut-down version. If you decide it isn't for you, do nothing and it simply ends.

ask: is it right for my subject
topics.answer:
It covers **KG through Grade 12**, and it knows the **MoE** and **IB** curricula. British, American and Indian curriculum schools use it too.

Subject doesn't really limit it — sciences, maths, languages, humanities. What matters more is that you can attach *your* syllabus or textbook chapter, so the draft follows the book your school actually teaches from rather than a generic one.

**English and Arabic**, both fully — including right-to-left layout across the whole interface, not just translated labels.

You can draft a lesson in one language and teach it in the other.

ask: what do you do with my data
topics.answer:
Your work is yours. A few specifics:

- Documents you upload go to **private storage scoped to your account** — nobody else's session can reach them.
- Your lesson plans and student records are visible to **you**, not to other teachers.
- Nothing you write is used to train a model.

If you need something specific for your school's policy, ask through the contact form and a person will answer.

Yes — that's the **My students** section.

- Build a register: students, grades and sections.
- Group them into classes.
- Take attendance; marking it twice corrects it rather than doubling it.
- Record marks by hand, or let scored work flow in from quizzes and homework you assigned.

The gradebook averages both together, so an average means what you'd expect.

ask: can i upload my own material
topics.answer:
Two places files matter:

- **Setting up your profile** — upload a CV or staff card and Murchid reads your name, subjects, grades and school off it. Two clicks instead of a form.
- **Making something** — attach a chapter, a syllabus or a worksheet and the draft is built from *that*, not from a generic template.

PDFs and photos both work.

ask: how do i create an account
can i sign in with google
topics.answer:
Press **Try the studio** at the top of the page.

You can sign in with **Google**, **LinkedIn**, or an email and password — same page for signing up and signing in, so you don't have to work out which you need.

With LinkedIn or a CV upload, your profile fills itself in.

ask: can i make the text bigger
topics.answer:
Yes, and it's right here — open the **Accessibility** tab at the top of this panel.

You'll find text size, a dyslexia-friendly typeface, letter and line spacing, high contrast, colour-blind filters, a larger cursor, and a switch to stop all animation. There are one-tap profiles for vision, dyslexia and motor needs too.

Whatever you set is remembered on this device.

ask: how do i use the microphone
topics.answer:
Yes, both ways.

- **Speak instead of typing** — press the microphone in the box below and talk.
- **Have replies read aloud** — press the speaker icon at the top of this panel.

It uses your browser's own speech, so your voice isn't uploaded anywhere. If you don't see a microphone, your browser doesn't support it — Chrome, Edge and Safari do; Firefox doesn't.

ask: can i talk to a person
topics.answer:
Use the contact form at the bottom of this page and a person will get back to you.

If something's actually broken, mention which screen you were on and what you were trying to do — it makes it much faster to fix.

Hello — good to see you.
